General surgery · published research

Intra-abdominal adhesions

One rat experiment found significantly lower macroscopic adhesion scores after seven days of near-infrared PBM. Antioxidant measures increased, but the short-term molecular and tissue findings do not establish fewer adhesions or complications in patients.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One rat experiment found significantly lower macroscopic adhesion scores after seven days of near-infrared PBM. Antioxidant measures increased, but the short-term molecular and tissue findings do not establish fewer adhesions or complications in patients.

Summary of the Evidence

One 2026 publication studied 96 male Wistar rats divided among eight groups of 12 after surgically induced abdominal adhesions. It compared PBM with control and several other interventions. This is one animal experiment, not eight separate studies; no human, cell-culture, or ex-vivo PBM study of intra-abdominal adhesions was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

No patient study has tested whether PBM prevents adhesions after abdominal surgery or reduces bowel obstruction, infertility, chronic pain, or repeat operations. The available evidence comes from short-term adhesion scores and laboratory measures in rats.

Animal evidence

PBM alone significantly reduced macroscopic adhesion scores compared with control at the study endpoint. The PBM group also showed the strongest reported antifibrotic effect, and antioxidant enzyme activities, including superoxide dismutase and catalase, increased. Histological and gene-expression analyses examined inflammation and tissue repair. The direct macroscopic result is favorable in this model, while its clinical meaning remains unknown (Okur et al. 2026).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No independent cell-culture or ex-vivo study was identified. The biochemical and gene-expression measurements were performed on rat samples from the same experiment.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The experiment used 904-nm near-infrared light at 3 J/cm², applied over the abdominal incision for 60 seconds once daily on seven consecutive days. The rat study did not compare multiple PBM doses or wavelengths. Its postoperative model and day-eight assessment cannot establish whether treatment changes later adhesion formation or clinical complications in people.

Interpretation

PBM reduced macroscopic adhesion scores in this single rat experiment, which is a direct positive result for the measured endpoint. The follow-up was short and no human study was identified, so it remains unknown whether the same treatment would prevent clinically consequential adhesions after surgery in people.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for reduced adhesion scores in an experimental rat model
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One 96-rat experiment found lower macroscopic adhesion scores after PBM alone and increased antioxidant enzyme activity. The study measured short-term tissue and laboratory outcomes, and some molecular markers did not align uniformly with the adhesion score. No human study or independent replication was identified. Replication with longer follow-up and clinically relevant complications is needed.
